• Belongs to the Betta foerschi complex.
  • IUCN Red List: N/A (no information available, but its status is suspected to be similar to that of B. foerschi, Endangered).
  • Wild caught.
  • Maximum size: 2.25 inches (about 5.7 cm).
  • Breeding: mouthbrooder.
These fish are a splendid as well as interesting enrichment for well maintained blackwater aquaria.

All species of the Betta foerschi complex are found only in Borneo: B. foerschi in the Mentaya River drainage, B. mandor in the lower Kapuas River drainage, and B. strohi about 30 km south of Sukamara; there is no major river named there (but nameless rivers do exist).

• TDS: ~60–100 (can tolerate high-TDS water but prefers low TDS).
  • pH: ~6.0–7.0 (prefers softer water).
  • Temperature: 75–83°F (about 24–28°C); does well at cooler temperatures, but higher temperatures bring out coloration and breeding behaviour.
Temperament: somewhat territorial, but can be kept in groups as long as there is enough space.

B. strohi is a reserved fish, which can be socialized very well with other peaceful blackwater fish, e.g. rasboras, chocolate gouramis, pearl gouramis etc. If you like, you can also keep several males together; they bicker, if at all, only harmlessly with each other.

Black-brown base body with red-gold bars on the opercular cheeks in both males and females. Adult males have longer anal and caudal fins than females. Very similar to B. foerschi, except that females have blue ventral fins. Like many species in the complex, females show vertical bars on the body when in breeding mode. B. mandor, B. foerschi and B. strohi are notoriously difficult to sex at a young age; older fish with longer finnage are much easier.
The sexes can be distinguished quite well by the extension of the fins.

The species status of Betta strohi is controversial. It is a form from the species complex around Betta foerschi. Some authors consider B. strohi to be a synonym of B. foerschi, others a valid species. Technically the two differ by a rather inconspicuous feature, namely the eye line. In Betta strohi the line runs from the gill cover through the eye, in B. foerschi it runs below the eye. In living animals this is hardly ever visible, but in preserved animals it is.

A very important feature is the coloration of the gill cover in mating animals. It is bright yellow in B. strohi and bright red in B. foerschi. If they are not in mating mood, the fish do not show it. However, this characteristic is also controversial: in the original description, animals of B. strohi have red gill cover stripes and B. foerschi yellow ones.
